html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Term Meaning
Monitoring Collecting, measuring and assessing data and trends; comparing actual with planned performance; producing performance measures; reporting performance information
Controlling Analyzing variances, assessing trends, evaluating alternatives, and recommending corrective or preventive action, replanning and follow-up until performance issues are resolved
Metric A description of a project or product attribute and how to measure it
Leading indicator Shows upcoming changes or trends (backlog in progress, no risk process, disengaged stakeholders, vague success criteria); lets you act before tolerance is crossed
Lagging indicator Reflects past performance (deliverables completed, schedule or cost variance, resources consumed); easier to measure
Input / output / outcome metric Input: what goes in (utilization, hours). Output: what is produced (features, velocity). Outcome: the value achieved (benefits, usage, satisfaction); governance prefers outcome metrics over input metrics
SMART Specific, measurable, achievable, realistic, time-bound
Work performance data → information → reports Raw observations → compared with plan and thresholds → compiled to generate decisions, actions or awareness (Topic 14)
Status report The current status: progress since the last report and forecasts for cost and schedule
Dashboard Charts and graphs showing progress against key measures, often red-amber-green (stoplight), with drill-down and text for measures outside thresholds
Information radiator / visual control A visible display (often low-tech) where people can see status at a glance (task board, Kanban board, burn chart); "visual controls" in lean environments
Cycle time / lead time Cycle time: from when a task starts until it is complete. Lead time: from when an item enters the board until delivery
Forecast A prediction of future cost, schedule or performance from current data and trends (EAC, schedule forecast)
Artifact A document or other item created to help manage the project and provide information to the team, stakeholders and management
Reconciliation Beyond PMBOK 8term Checking that figures agree across sources (accounting vs project costs, reported progress vs accepted work) and use consistent definitions

2Monitor and Control Project Performance (the process)

Purpose (PMBOK 8): track, review and report overall progress to meet the performance objectives in the plan, so stakeholders understand the current state, see the actions taken on performance issues, and see forecasts of cost and schedule. It also evaluates whether decisions might enhance the value proposition; if a beneficial decision changes a baseline, integrated change control is used (Topic 29).

It involves: evaluating performance against the plan; tracking resource utilization, work completed and budget spent; demonstrating accountability; informing stakeholders; assessing whether deliverables are on track to deliver planned benefits; discussing trade-offs, threats, opportunities and options; evaluating current risks, finding new ones and monitoring responses; ensuring deliverables will meet customer acceptance criteria; and updating the sourcing strategy.

Aspect Detail
Inputs Plan components, assumption log, basis of estimates, cost and schedule forecasts, issue log, lessons learned, milestone list, quality reports, risk register and report, work performance information, agreements, EEFs, OPAs
Tools Expert judgment; data analysis (alternative analysis, cost-benefit, earned value, root cause, trend and variance analysis); decision-making (voting); meetings; project dashboards, visual controls, information radiators
Outputs Work performance reports, change requests, plan updates, document updates (cost and schedule forecasts, issue log, lessons learned register, risk register)
Measurement mindset Measure only what is relevant and actionable (time and effort are limited); metrics should meet SMART criteria

3Develop Project Metrics, Analysis and Reconciliation (ECO)

Governance needs three components (PMBOK 8 §2.1.3): target metrics aligned with strategic goals; signaling mechanisms (typically leading indicators) that show whether delivery is moving toward the goal; and feedback mechanisms so decision-makers learn and improve their decisions. Governance examples: effectiveness of prioritization (ROI), due-date performance, and whether the current integrated baseline carries the highest value.

How to build the metric set:

  1. Start from the success criteria and objectives (Topic 12) and benefits plan (Topic 10): what must be true for the project to succeed?
  2. Choose a balanced few: outcomes and outputs, leading and lagging, process and product.
  3. Make each metric SMART, with a definition, source, owner, frequency, baseline or target and threshold for action.
  4. Tailor to the approach (below) and to stakeholder needs.
  5. Reconcile: confirm the data are consistent across sources and use the same definitions (project cost vs accounting records, reported progress vs accepted work), before they are reported.
  6. Review and retire: drop metrics nobody uses and those that mislead.

Typical metrics by domain [examples]:

Domain Examples
Scope Scope definition accuracy, requirements stability, scope creep percentage, acceptance rate (Topic 15)
Schedule SV, SPI, milestone variance, velocity, burn charts, cycle time, percent complete (Topic 16)
Finance CV, CPI, EAC, TCPI, spend per iteration vs value (Topic 17)
Quality Defects (found and escaped), test coverage, rework, cost of quality (Topic 18)
Resources Utilization, downtime, turnover, team satisfaction (Topic 19)
Stakeholders Satisfaction, engagement, Net Promoter Score (Topic 13)
Risk Open high risks, exposure, reserve use, issues (Topic 21)
Benefits and value Benefits realized, ROI, adoption and usage (Topic 10)

4Measurement Pitfalls (PMBOK 8)

Pitfall What happens What to do
Hawthorne effect Measuring changes behavior; output-only measures push volume over customer value Include outcome measures (satisfaction, usage)
Vanity metric Looks good but does not inform decisions (page views vs new users) Choose metrics tied to decisions
Demoralization Unachievable targets make morale fall Set stretch goals but recognize progress
Misusing metrics Gaming: favoring less-important or short-term measures, or doing easy out-of-sequence work to move an indicator Balance short- and long-term metrics; watch behavior
Confirmation bias Seeing only data that support existing views Seek disconfirming evidence
Correlation vs causation Assuming one variable causes another Look for other factors (estimating skill, change control, risk management)

Exam patterns: a team meets its velocity targets but clients rarely use the features: shift to usage and outcome measures. Progress counted by installs while customer issues spike: include quality and outcome in progress. Steady velocity can hide falling morale; investigate. A burnup showing scope growth explains slow completion without blaming the team.

5Assess Current Progress and Analyze Performance (ECO)

Technique Use
Performance reviews Compare actual work in progress with the schedule baseline: actual start and finish dates, percent complete, remaining duration
Variance analysis Cause and degree of difference between baseline and actual; view cost, time, technical and resource variances together; decide preventive or corrective action
Trend analysis Forecast results from history; early warning of slippage
Earned value Integrate scope, cost and schedule: PV, EV, AC, CV, SV, CPI, SPI, EAC, TCPI (Topics 17 and 34)
Burn charts, velocity, cycle time Adaptive progress: burndown (remaining work vs time left), burnup (completed work vs total scope), accepted work per iteration
Root cause analysis Find why before deciding what to do (Topic 18)
Regression and predictive analytics Relate variables to outcomes; ML on historical data to forecast risks and performance (with human review)
Milestone and acceptance status Deliverables accepted vs planned; quality and benefit indicators

From analysis to action: compare with thresholds set in the plans; if outside, find the cause, forecast, evaluate options (corrective or preventive action, reserves, scope or schedule change), raise change requests where baselines change, escalate beyond authority, and report (Topics 17 and 29).

6Communicate Project Status (ECO)

  • Know the audience and the decision: sponsor (summary, forecasts, risks and decisions needed), governance board (the formats and metrics it requires, for example earned value), team (daily boards), customers (demos, release information), regulators (formal reports) (Topic 20).
  • Content: progress since the last report; forecasts of cost and schedule; scope and change status; quality and benefit indicators; key risks and issues; decisions or support needed; next period.
  • Dashboards: red-amber-green status with a text explanation for any measure outside its threshold; drill-down for detail; avoid decoration.
  • Visual controls and radiators: put status where stakeholders can see it, not only in the team's space.
  • Cadence: regular reports plus exception reports when thresholds are crossed; agree formats and frequency for each audience in advance (for example monthly to the CFO and quarterly to the board, each defined).
  • Be accurate and timely: show facts and trends, include bad news early with options; do not let green hide a known problem.
  • New sponsor or key stakeholder: brief them and reconfirm objectives and support, rather than just sending the latest report.
  • Support governance: provide what the board requires; agree one reporting structure when several bodies ask (Topic 20).

7Artifacts: Identify, Tailor, Maintain, Make Accessible, Assess (ECO)

PMBOK 8 context: the processes list a sampling of artifacts (inputs and outputs); they are illustrative, not prescriptive, and each organization tailors them. Plans, baselines, project documents, reports and deliverables are all artifacts. The configuration management plan says which artifacts are under configuration control; changes to those need a formal change request. Baselines change only through change control; project documents are updated as work proceeds.

Enabler What to do
Identify and tailor needed artifacts Start from OPA templates; select the artifacts that add value for the project's size, complexity, risk, regulation, development approach and audience; omit or simplify the rest. A tiny agile project may need a backlog, board and a few registers; a regulated project needs more
Create, review, update and document Give each artifact an owner, template and cadence; review for completeness and accuracy; update as work proceeds (a risk register last updated at kickoff is a red flag); record versions, approvals and decisions; capture lessons continuously; keep roadmaps and backlogs current as releases reveal value
Help ensure accessibility One controlled repository or PMIS with permissions, version control and search; approved versions easy to find (auditors should not hunt through personal drives); pull access for large audiences, information radiators for team and stakeholders; security and confidentiality respected; accessible formats and languages for audiences
Continually assess effectiveness of artifact management Are artifacts used? Do they inform decisions? What do they cost to maintain? Ask stakeholders; keep what is used and retire, merge or simplify the rest (do not merge unused content into one bigger report)
Update organizational assets When a project produces a proven procedure or better template, update the organization's library or OPAs, not only the project log (Topic 31)

8Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Progress Percent complete, earned value, milestones against the baseline Accepted working increments, burn charts, velocity, cycle time, flow Milestones for the envelope; burn charts inside
Metrics SPI, CPI, variances, thresholds, quality and benefit indicators Value delivered, usage, defects escaped, team health, forecast release dates Both
Visibility Status reports, dashboards, steering packs Information radiators, task boards, sprint reviews, demos Both
Cadence Monthly or phase-based, plus exception reports Every iteration and continuously Both
Artifacts More formal plans and logs; configuration control Lightweight: backlog, board, working agreements, a few logs; roadmap updated each release Formal envelope, light inside
Pitfall Reporting activity instead of outcomes Reporting output (velocity) instead of value Mixed signals

9Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

  • Tailor metrics, reporting depth, cadence and artifacts to size, criticality, regulation, culture, number of stakeholders and development approach.
  • Interactions: status draws on every domain (scope acceptance, schedule and cost performance, quality, resources, stakeholder satisfaction, risk, benefits) and feeds governance, change control and communication.
  • Check results (Table 2-5): project metrics are in place and tracked regularly; key management members are kept apprised of operational status, resource needs, risks and response plans, assumptions, benefits realized, decision criteria, change control, compliance, communication, issues and funding.

10Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Report in the form governance needs (for example earned value) and agree formats with each audience; do not reuse one format for all.
  2. Output is not value. Velocity, features and installs are outputs; track usage, benefits and outcomes too.
  3. Progress must include quality and outcome (installs that work, accepted increments), not only counts.
  4. Prefer leading indicators to prevent problems; use lagging indicators to learn and find correlations.
  5. SPI and CPI together: an SPI above 1 with a CPI below 1 means speed was bought; analyze causes and report through governance.
  6. Forecast with the EAC, not the BAC (Topic 17).
  7. Watch the pitfalls: Hawthorne effect, vanity metrics, gaming, confirmation bias, correlation vs causation.
  8. Keep artifacts current and findable: a controlled repository, a review cadence, owners.
  9. Tailor and prune artifacts: keep what stakeholders use; retire or simplify the rest.
  10. Update organizational assets when a project proves a better procedure.
  11. Explain red and amber with causes, actions and decisions needed; do not report only colors.
  12. Show the real cause of slow progress (a burnup with growing scope) instead of pressuring the team.
  13. Brief a new sponsor and reconfirm objectives.
  14. Reconcile data and definitions before reporting.
  15. Use baselines and thresholds: variance within tolerance is monitored; beyond it triggers analysis and action.
  16. Keep the roadmap and backlog alive as each release teaches something new.

11Exam Q&A

11.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1The project manager of an agile program wants an early warning of delivery trouble rather than a record of past performance. Which signals are leading indicators?

  • AGrowing work in progress and stakeholders who stop attending reviews
  • BThe defects found and fixed during the previous release of the product
  • CLast month's schedule variance and the cost variance to date
  • DThe number of deliverables completed and the hours consumed so far
Show the answer

Answer: A. Leading indicators reveal upcoming changes or trends, for example growing work in progress, disengaged stakeholders, no risk process or poorly defined success criteria. Variances, completed deliverables and resources consumed describe past performance.

S2While reviewing survey results about two vendors, the project manager notices that only the comments supporting the vendor already favored are being highlighted. Which pitfall is this, and what is the remedy?

  • AHawthorne effect; stop surveying the stakeholders so they cannot change behavior
  • BConfirmation bias; look for evidence that contradicts the preferred view
  • CVanity metric; replace the survey with a count of the comments received
  • DDemoralization; lower the survey's targets so that the team stays motivated
Show the answer

Answer: B. Seeing only the data that support an existing view is confirmation bias, and the remedy is to seek disconfirming evidence. The other pitfalls concern metrics that do not inform decisions, behavior that changes when measured, or unachievable targets.

S3A review shows that late projects also tend to run over budget, and a manager concludes that lateness causes overruns. What should the project manager recommend?

  • AAccept the conclusion and require every late project to submit a cost recovery plan
  • BTreat the overruns as the cause of lateness and increase the budgets
  • CStop tracking cost, since schedule performance alone explains the budget results
  • DLook for other factors, such as estimating skill, change control and risk management
Show the answer

Answer: D. Two variables moving together does not prove that one causes the other; other factors such as poor estimating, weak change control or inadequate risk management may drive both. Accepting causation, dropping cost tracking or reversing the assumption repeats the error.

S4To raise the "tickets closed" figure, a Kanban support team closes easy tickets first while critical tickets age. Which pitfall is this, and what is the response?

  • AMisusing metrics; balance it with ticket age and priority
  • BVanity metric; replace the measure with the number of tickets received
  • CConfirmation bias; collect more data that supports the team's current approach
  • DCorrelation versus causation; look for another cause of the aging tickets
Show the answer

Answer: A. Gaming a metric by favoring easy or out-of-sequence work to move an indicator is misuse of metrics, addressed by balancing short- and long-term measures and watching behavior. The other pitfalls do not describe choosing easy work to move the figure.

S5The sponsor demands a recovery plan for a 4% schedule slip, while the plan's control threshold is plus or minus 10%. What should the project manager do?

  • ALeave the variance out of the report because it is within the threshold
  • BExplain that it is within tolerance and keep monitoring against the threshold
  • CPrepare a full recovery plan immediately, since the sponsor has requested it
  • DRaise a change request to widen the threshold to 15% to avoid further requests
Show the answer

Answer: B. Variances inside the thresholds in the plan are monitored, and those beyond them trigger analysis and action. The sponsor is told openly, so omitting the variance, preparing unnecessary recovery or widening the threshold unilaterally misuses the control mechanism.

S6A six-person agile team is told to produce all fourteen artifacts on the organization's standard template list. What should the project manager do?

  • ASelect the artifacts that add value for this project and tailor or omit the rest
  • BProduce the fourteen artifacts but update them only at the end of the project
  • CProduce none of them, because agile teams do not create any documents
  • DProduce all fourteen, since the template list is the organization's standard
Show the answer

Answer: A. Artifacts are illustrative, not prescriptive: they are selected and tailored to the project's size, risk, approach and audience, starting from OPA templates. Producing everything, nothing or stale versions fails to add value.

S7A business analyst edits an approved requirements specification directly on the shared drive to improve a section, and nobody is told. Which practice was missed?

  • AQuality audit, with auditors approving the wording of each requirement
  • BResource leveling, with the analyst's workload spread over several weeks
  • CStakeholder analysis, with every reader of the specification surveyed
  • DConfiguration control, with a change request for controlled artifacts
Show the answer

Answer: D. Artifacts under configuration control change only through a formal change request, with versions recorded and the current approved version identified. Audits, leveling and stakeholder analysis are different activities.

S8Which of these is a SMART metric for a support team?

  • AMake the quality of the product the best that it can possibly be
  • BReduce average defect fix time from 6 days to 4 days by 30 September
  • CImprove the handling of defects much faster during the coming months
  • DFix defects as fast as possible, with no limit on the effort required
Show the answer

Answer: B. A SMART metric is specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound, and a named baseline, target and date makes the first option measurable. The others are vague, open-ended or unbounded.

S9A project shows an SPI of 0.9 and a CPI of 1.1. What is the most reasonable first interpretation?

  • AOn schedule and on budget, since the two indices offset each other
  • BAhead of schedule and over budget, so costs are the main concern
  • CBehind schedule and under budget, possibly because work is understaffed
  • DBehind schedule and over budget, so both baselines need to be reset
Show the answer

Answer: C. An SPI below 1 means behind schedule and a CPI above 1 means under budget, a combination that can arise when work is delayed or understaffed so that less is spent than planned. The indices do not offset each other, and neither baseline needs resetting on this evidence alone.

S10The project manager of a hybrid program keeps the status green because the milestone is still three weeks away, although the key supplier has just announced a six-week delay. What should the project manager do?

  • AReport amber without any explanation, to avoid alarming the stakeholders
  • BKeep green until the milestone date actually passes, then report the delay
  • CUpdate the status to reflect the forecast, with causes, options and decisions needed
  • DWait for the supplier to confirm the delay in writing before saying anything
Show the answer

Answer: C. Status reports show facts and forecasts, and bad news is shared early with options, so a known six-week delay must be reflected now. Waiting for the date, reporting a color without causes or waiting for paperwork lets green hide a known problem.

11.2 Recall Q&As

R1What is the difference between leading and lagging indicators?

Show the answer

Leading indicators show upcoming changes or trends and allow prevention; lagging indicators reflect past performance and are easier to measure.

R2What do SMART criteria stand for?

Show the answer

Specific, measurable, achievable, realistic, time-bound.

R3Name the measurement pitfalls in PMBOK 8.

Show the answer

Hawthorne effect, vanity metrics, demoralization, misusing metrics, confirmation bias, correlation vs causation.

R4What three components does effective governance typically need?

Show the answer

Target metrics aligned with strategy, signaling mechanisms (leading indicators), and feedback mechanisms.

R5What does Monitor and Control Project Performance output?

Show the answer

Work performance reports, change requests, plan and document updates (forecasts, issue log, lessons learned, risk register).

R6What is a dashboard, and how should out-of-threshold items be shown?

Show the answer

Charts and graphs of progress against key measures (often red-amber-green); add a text explanation for measures outside thresholds.

R7What is an information radiator or visual control?

Show the answer

A visible display of status (task board, burn chart) placed where people can see it.

R8Cycle time versus lead time?

Show the answer

Cycle time runs from the start of a task to completion; lead time from when an item enters the board to delivery.

R9Why reconcile data?

Show the answer

To make sure figures agree across sources and definitions before reporting.

R10What does the configuration management plan do for artifacts?

Show the answer

It specifies which artifacts are under configuration control; changes to them require a formal change request.

R11How should needed artifacts be chosen?

Show the answer

By tailoring OPA templates to size, complexity, risk, regulation, approach and audience, keeping what adds value.

R12What makes artifacts accessible?

Show the answer

A controlled repository or PMIS with permissions, version control and search so approved versions are easy to find.

R13How do you assess the effectiveness of artifact management?

Show the answer

Check whether artifacts are used, inform decisions and are worth their maintenance cost; keep what is used and retire or simplify the rest.

R14What does a status report contain?

Show the answer

Progress since the last report and forecasts for cost and schedule, with other status information.

12Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Monitoring vs controlling Measure, compare, report vs analyze, decide corrective or preventive action, follow up
Metrics SMART; balanced; outcomes over inputs; leading and lagging; thresholds
Governance metrics Target metrics, signaling (leading), feedback
Pitfalls Hawthorne, vanity, demoralization, gaming, confirmation bias, correlation vs causation
Progress Predictive: EV, milestones; adaptive: accepted increments, burn charts, velocity
Analysis Performance reviews, variance, trend, EV, root cause, forecasts
Reports Tailored; forecasts; RAG with explanations; exception reports; agreed formats
Visual controls Boards, burn charts, radiators visible to stakeholders
Artifacts Tailor, create, review, update, control, make accessible, assess, retire
Repository Controlled, versioned, searchable; approved versions findable
Effectiveness Used? Informs decisions? Worth the cost?
Org assets Update libraries and templates with proven improvements
Reconciliation Consistent data and definitions across sources
First-action pattern Check thresholds, find the cause, forecast, report to the audience's needs, use change control, keep artifacts current and findable
